chief_complaint: hives and vomiting immediately after eating peanut butter
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with hives and vomiting immediately after eating peanut butter. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the jar of peanut butter was rancid, expired, or contaminated with foodborne bacteria like salmonella.
concerns: He is worried that an accidental trace of peanuts hidden in restaurant food could trigger an even worse attack and kill him before help arrives.
expectations: He hopes to get allergy testing to confirm what happened, a prescription for an emergency self-injector pen, and a list of foods to avoid.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Peanut Allergy (IgE-mediated food allergy) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Peanut Allergy (IgE-mediated food allergy) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

The current reaction is systemic and should be treated as anaphylaxis with immediate intramuscular epinephrine and emergency evaluation; after recovery, management includes strict peanut avoidance and an epinephrine auto-injector.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: hives and vomiting immediately after eating peanut butter

Key HPI features: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with hives and vomiting immediately after eating peanut butter. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Peanut Allergy.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Peanut Allergy (IgE-mediated food allergy).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Oral allergy syndrome (localized, milder) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any airway or breathing symptoms accompanying the reaction — this becomes anaphylaxis.
management_principles: Treat the current systemic reaction with intramuscular epinephrine and emergency evaluation; after recovery, institute strict peanut avoidance and prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Peanut Allergy
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Peanut Allergy
Implement evidence-based management plan: Treat systemic reactions with intramuscular epinephrine; after recovery, use strict peanut avoidance and an epinephrine auto-injector

teaching.one_liner: An IgE-mediated allergy to peanut protein causing rapid-onset hives, vomiting, or worse after ingestion — requires strict avoidance and an epinephrine auto-injector.
red_flags: Any airway or breathing symptoms accompanying the reaction — this becomes anaphylaxis

must_ask.say: What did you eat, and how soon did symptoms start?
Did you have hives, vomiting, or any trouble breathing?
Is this the first time, or has this happened before with peanuts?
Did the symptoms get worse quickly, or stay mild?
Do you already avoid peanuts, and do you carry emergency medication?

history.answer: I started breaking out in itchy red welts all over my body and threw up right after eating peanut butter toast about an hour ago.
The hives started about fifteen minutes after I ate the toast, and they have been spreading quickly across my chest, belly, and arms.
They started on my chest and stomach and then popped up over my back and both arms.
They look like swollen red patches and hives with pale centers, like giant mosquito bites.
It is intensely itchy and feels warm, but there is no burning or tender skin pain.
Some earlier spots fade a bit, but new red welts keep appearing in other areas.
I threw up twice shortly after the hives appeared, bringing up everything I ate, and now I feel completely wiped out.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or general body aches.
No sores, blisters, or raw spots in my mouth, eyes, or private areas.
No, my skin is intact and not peeling, and there are no dark purple spots or bruises.
My lips tingled a little, but my throat does not feel tight and I am breathing normally without wheezing.
I feel weak from vomiting, but I have not felt faint, lightheaded, or dizzy when standing.
No, I have not started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, or pain medications lately.
I ate two slices of toast with a new jar of peanut butter about an hour ago; I have not used new soaps, lotions, or colognes.
No bug bites, tick encounters, hiking, or travel recently.
No, my wife and everyone at my office are completely fine.
I get mild seasonal stuffy nose in the spring, but I have never had asthma, eczema, or diagnosed food allergies.
No joint swelling, joint pain, or changes in my fingernails.
I have not applied any steroid creams, lotions, or ointments; I came straight to the clinic after vomiting.
I am in a committed relationship with my wife and have no history of genital sores or sexually transmitted infections.
I used to eat peanuts when I was younger without any problem, so I have never experienced a reaction like this before.
The reaction escalated quickly over the past hour, going from mild itching to widespread hives and vomiting.
I do not carry an EpiPen or allergy medicines because I never had this happen, but I will strictly avoid all peanuts now.

I thought the jar of peanut butter must have gone bad or had salmonella in it to make me vomit and break out like that. I'm terrified that if I accidentally eat even a tiny trace of nuts at a restaurant, my throat will close and I could die before an ambulance arrives.
I have no chronic medical conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart trouble.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
None. I do not take any regular prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend, but I have not had any alcohol today.
I work as an office administrator and live with my wife in an apartment.
My mother has mild asthma, but nobody in my family has serious food allergies or anaphylaxis.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert, mildly fatigued male in moderate distress from pruritus and nausea, sitting comfortably without tachypnea or accessory muscle use.

Multiple erythematous, raised, edematous wheals of varying sizes with central pallor distributed over the chest, abdomen, back, and both arms, all blanching completely with no purpura, blisters, or skin detachment.
Conjunctivae are clear without injection or pallor, and sclerae are anicteric without periorbital edema.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink without angioedema of the lips, tongue, or uvula, and the posterior pharynx is patent without swelling.
No lymphadenopathy palpable in the anterior or posterior cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular chains.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no audible wheezing, rhonchi, or stridor.
Regular rate and rhythm with mild tachycardia; normal S1 and S2 present without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and mildly tender diffusely without localized guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness.
